title: The hardening fix that locked everyone out
subtitle: Reversing my own security change within a day, because the threat model said a different control was the one that mattered

stats.label: holes the review found; the worst, anonymous registration with attacker-chosen redirects
acceptance probes, one or more for each fix
from adding the registration lock to reverting it

lede: A security review of my deliberately public OAuth endpoint found holes, the worst of them in client registration. I fixed all three, checked the fixes with explicit probes, and the next morning every AI assistant that used the endpoint could no longer authenticate. I re-ran the threat model. The registration lock had added friction without adding security, because the control that protects is the consent screen, where I log in and approve every grant. I reverted my own fix and wrote down why. The endpoint exists so that AI assistants, including commercial ones, can connect to my private tool estate.
quote: The consent screen is the control. Registration is bookkeeping.
evidence: Security incident judgment: I reverted my own registration lock within 24 h of adding it, after it locked every AI assistant out and the threat model showed consent was the control.
OAuth 2.0 and identity architecture: a deliberately public endpoint where AI assistants self-register as clients and a person approves every grant on the consent screen.
Security review triage: 3 findings fixed in severity order with minimal changes, each fix checked by acceptance probes, 7 in all.
Threat modelling for AI client access: a hostile registration shown to gain nothing unless a person approves that client on the consent screen.
author: Corey James
